rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hereafter exposes earthly time as an illusion of human experience, without bearing on ultimate reality.
rows.anchor: the illusory concept of "time" as experienced by the human mind - a concept which has no bearing on the ultimate reality

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad points to 6:47, note 37, for a parallel statement.
rows.anchor: Cf. the last sentence of 6:47 and the corresponding note 37.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah takes its designation from the letter-symbol qaf placed before its first verse.
rows.anchor: KNOWN only by the letter-symbol q (qaf) preceding th e first verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad dates the surah to the fourth year of the Prophet's mission.
rows.anchor: this surah appears to have been revealed in the fourth year of the Prophet's mission

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Framed by references to the Qur'an at its beginning and end, the surah treats death and resurrection.
rows.anchor: Commencing and ending with a reference to the Qur'an, it is devoted in its entirety to the twin problems of death and resurrection.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The instruction to bear patiently concerns claims that resurrection is impossible.
rows.anchor: regarding the alleged 'impossibility' of resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Glorifying God before sunrise and sunset means remembering His almightiness throughout the day.
rows.anchor: remember His almightiness at all times of day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad dates the surah to about seven years before the Prophet's hijrah.
rows.anchor: this surah was revealed about seven years before the Prophet's hijrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mawqi can mean the time, place, or manner at which something comes down; Asad also renders the phrase as the stars' setting or orbiting.
rows.anchor: at which something comes down

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators take the phrase to refer to the stars breaking apart at the Last Hour.
rows.anchor: many of the commentators think that the phrase mawaqi an-nujum relates to the break-up of the stars at the Last Hour

rows.speaker: Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and As-Suddi
rows.claim: They interpret the phrase as the Qur'an's gradual, step-by-step revelation, a reading supported by the following verses.
rows.anchor: Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and As-Suddi were definitely of the opinion, strongly supported by the subsequent verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gradual revelation over twenty-three years points to the Qur'an's freedom from inconsistency despite dramatic changes in the Prophet's life; this explains the parenthetic emphasis in verse 76.
rows.anchor: By "calling to witness" the gradual manner of its revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mention of iron and its implications made the surah known as the one in which iron is mentioned, as Tabari reports.
rows.anchor: THE MENTION in verse 25 of "iron"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reference to the conquest of Mecca places the earliest possible revelation at the end of 8 AH.
rows.anchor: From the reference to the conquest of Mecca (al-fath) in verse 10 it is obvious that the earliest date of its revelation would be the end of the year 8 H.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi stresses that worldly life is not intrinsically contemptible: God created it meaningfully, and it is a positive gift and potential source of blessings.
rows.anchor: Razi makes it clear that life as such is not to be despised, inasmuch as it has been created by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Life loses its positive quality when pursued recklessly, without regard for spiritual values or the hereafter.
rows.anchor: it loses this positive quality if it is indulged in recklessly, blindly and with disregard of spiritual values and considerations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording is literally, 'like the parable of ...'.
rows.anchor: Lit., "[It is] like the parable of ..., etc.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the Qur'an's only use of kuffar in its original sense of tillers; Asad points to its etymology and the later sense of deniers in 74:10.
rows.anchor: original meaning of "tiller of the soil"

rows.speaker: Tabari
rows.claim: Tabari takes the conjunction wa here to mean aw, 'or'.
rows.anchor: According to Tabari, the conjunction wa has here the meaning of aw ("or").

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most of the surah concerns the conflict between the Muslim community and Medina's Jewish Banu 'n-Nadir and their expulsion.
rows.anchor: MOST of this surah (i.e., verses 2-17) refers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the Hijrah, the Prophet made a neutrality treaty with Banu 'n-Nadir; after Badr its leaders recognized Muhammad as the foretold prophet, but after Uhud they broke the pact and allied with Quraysh.
rows.anchor: After the Muslim victory in the battle of Badr

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet offered them war or departure with their possessions, with annual access to harvest their date groves if they chose to leave; they requested and received ten days.
rows.anchor: either war or departure from Medina with all their possessions. If they accepted this latter proposition, they would be allowed to return every year to gather the produce of their date groves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: During the respite they secretly conspired with Medina's hypocrites, led by Ibn Ubayy, who promised two thousand armed supporters and joint resistance or departure.
rows.anchor: led by 'Abd Allah ibn Ubay y, who promised them armed support

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Banu 'n-Nadir rejected the advice and armed themselves; after a 21-day siege without fighting and no promised aid, they surrendered in Rabi al-Awwal 4 AH.
rows.anchor: surrendered in the month of Rabi al-Awwal, 4 H.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The peace allowed them to take movable property but not arms; most left for Syria, while a few settled in Khaybar or traveled to al-Hirah.
rows.anchor: they would leave Medina, taking with them all their movable properties, but not their arms. Most of them emigrated to Syria in a caravan of about six hundred camels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their fields and plantations were forfeited, mostly assigned to needy Muslims, with the remainder reserved for the Muslim community.
rows.anchor: fields and plantations were forfeited

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The history illustrates that believers can triumph despite inferior numbers, wealth, and equipment when they remain conscious of God.
rows.anchor: believers - even if they are inferior in numbers, wealth and equipment - are bound to triumph over their opponents so long as they remain truly conscious of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conventional title echoes the gathering for war in verse 2; some Companions, including Ibn 'Abbas, called it Surat Bani 'n-Nadir.
rows.anchor: some of the Prophet's Companions - e.g., Ibn 'Abbas - used to refer to it as Surat Bani 'n-Nadir (Tabari)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad dates the surah to 4 AH.
rows.anchor: The date of revelation is the year 4 H.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most of the surah was revealed shortly after Uhud, in late 3 or early 4 AH, and addresses hypocrisy in the early Medinan community.
rows.anchor: shortly after the battle of Uhud

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although rooted in the Prophet's early Medinan circumstances, the Qur'anic lessons about hypocrisy apply in every time and circumstance.
rows.anchor: the Qur'anic treatment of this problem renders its lessons applicable to all times and circumstances

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to surah 2, note 4, for the related explanation.
rows.anchor: See surah 2, note 4.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means asking for a postponement for a near term.
rows.anchor: Lit., "for (ila) a term close-by".

rows.speaker: majority of commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators classify the surah as Medinan.
rows.anchor: The majority of the commentators regard this surah as belonging to the Medina period

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators instead consider it a late Meccan revelation.
rows.anchor: many others are of the opinion that it is a late Meccan revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word taghabun in verse 9 became the surah's identifying keyword.
rows.anchor: The expression taghabun, occurring in verse 9, has become the key-word by which this surah is designated.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An added 'time' is needed to make sense of the accusative yawma in the following phrase.
rows.anchor: This or a similar interpolation is necessary in view of the mansub form

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mid-Medinan surah elaborates divorce waiting-period rules before a final dissolution and remarriage, amplifying al-Baqarah 2:228-233.
rows.anchor: the waiting-period which divorced women must undergo before the marriage is finally dissolved and they are allowed to remarry

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means spending 'out of' one's means.
rows.anchor: Lit., "out of".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad places the surah probably third in revelation order and calls it one of the oldest Qur'anic portions.
rows.anchor: In the chronological order of revelation, this surah most probably occupies the third place

rows.speaker: Suyuti
rows.claim: Suyuti holds that the surah followed immediately after the first five verses of surah 96; Asad says this conflicts with the best-authenticated reports that most of surah 74 came second.
rows.anchor: Some authorities - among them Suyuti - incline to the view that it was revealed immediately after the first five verses of surah 96

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God tests the garden owners by giving them affluence far beyond their moral deserts.
rows.anchor: by bestowing on them affluence out of all proportion to their moral deserts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They planned without saying 'if God wills'; this is the parable's first lesson and links it to the question about their wealth in vv.14-15.
rows.anchor: which points to the first lesson to be derived from this parable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since Biblical times the poor have been understood to possess a right to a share of the harvest, as 6:141 states.
rows.anchor: the poor have a right to a share in the harvest of the fields and gardens owned by their more fortunate fellow-men

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The owners' resolve to deny the poor this right is the parable's second, specifically social, sin and connects with vv.10-13.
rows.anchor: the second type of sin to which the above parable points: and inasmuch as it is a social sin, it connects with verses 10-13

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The right-minded brother refers to the owners' failure to see that nothing happens unless God wills it.
rows.anchor: their failure to realize that nothing can come about unless the Almighty so wills

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Named for al-ma'arij in verse 3, this middle-Meccan surah treats unbelief's challenge to faith as conditioned by human restlessness.
rows.anchor: It is mainly devoted to the challenge which unbelief - or, rather, unwillingness to believe - offers to faith, both of them being conditioned by the restlessness inherent in human nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inborn restlessness can lead to achievement or discontent; verses 20-21 show its negative use, while prayerful moral consciousness turns it toward growth, stability, and contentment.
rows.anchor: an inner restlessness which may equally well drive him to fruitful achievement or to chronic discontent and frustration

rows.speaker: Jawhari
rows.claim: Jazu combines impatience with lamenting one's misfortune, making it the opposite of sabr.
rows.anchor: The participle jazu - derived from the verb jazi'a - combines the concepts of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-musallin here means people whose prayer reflects an underlying spiritual need and mindset, not ritual performance alone; this rightly directs restlessness to spiritual growth and releases self-pity and selfishness.
rows.anchor: does not relate here to the mere ritual of prayer but, rather, as the next verse shows, to the attitude of mind and the spiritual need underlying it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad places revelation no later than the final two years of the Prophet's Meccan sojourn and says the title comes from al-jinn in verse 1.
rows.anchor: this surah takes its name from the plural noun al-jinn in the first verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad regards this as probably the fourth revelation and says the whole surah belongs to early Mecca, though some verses may be later.
rows.anchor: THIS SURAH is almost certainly the fourth in the order of revelation

rows.speaker: some authorities
rows.claim: Some authorities call verse 20 Medinan; Asad says this claim has no substance.
rows.anchor: The contention of some authorities that verse 20 was revealed at Medina lacks all substance

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi reads all four torments as spiritual consequences: attachment to bodily pleasures shackles the soul and blocks purity, frustration burns, deprivation chokes, and separation from God's light and the blessed is grievous.
rows.anchor: Explaining this symbolism of torment in the hereafter, Razi says: "These four conditions may well be understood as denoting the spiritual consequences

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the first five verses of surah 96, revelation paused for an uncertain six months to three years, deeply distressing the Prophet and making him fear his first experience was illusory.
rows.anchor: AFTER the Prophet's earliest revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khadijah's support sustained the Prophet; after his vision of Gabriel, revelation became intense and continuous, as Bukhari and Muslim report.
rows.anchor: revelation became intense and continuous

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad places the surah at the beginning of the Meccan mission despite the possibility that some verses came later, and sees it as outlining the Qur'an's central themes: God, resurrection, moral responsibility, and afterlife as consequences of earthly conduct.
rows.anchor: the surah outlines almost all the fundamental concepts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revealed in the first third of the Meccan period, the surah focuses on resurrection except for the parenthetical vv.16-19.
rows.anchor: this surah is devoted almost entirely

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: The phrase means all the good and bad deeds one performed or omitted.
rows.anchor: whatever good and bad deeds he committed or omitted (Zamakhshari)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Early commentators disagree whether the surah, also called Ad-Dahr after verse 1, is Meccan or Medinan.
rows.anchor: THE OPINIONS of the earliest commentators are divided as to whether this surah

rows.speaker: Mujahid, Qatadah, Al-Hasan al-Basri and 'Ikrimah
rows.claim: These second-generation authorities, quoted by Baghawi, hold that the surah was revealed at Medina.
rows.anchor: among them Mujahid, Qatadah, Al-Hasan al-Basri and 'Ikrimah (all of them quoted by Baghawi) - hold the view that it was revealed at Medina

rows.speaker: classical commentators
rows.claim: The classical commentators take hal positively as qad: an immensely long or endless span of time has indeed passed.
rows.anchor: the interrogative particle hal having here the positive meaning of qad

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says the same sense can be conveyed by inserting 'not' into the question.
rows.anchor: this meaning can be brought out equally well by interpolating the word "not"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A 'thing mentionable' means nonexistent even as a hypothetical concept, refuting the anthropocentric claim that man rather than a Supreme Being is life's center and ultimate reality.
rows.anchor: non-existent even as a hypothetical concept. The purport of this statement is a refutation of the blasphemous "anthropocentric" world-view

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering God's name means recalling His attributes as manifested in creation; human beings can grasp His existence and attributes, but not the nature of His Reality, as Razi explains.
rows.anchor: His "attributes" as they manifest themselves in His creation - since the human mind can grasp only the fact of His existence and the manifestation of those "attributes"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad identifies the surah as late Meccan (following Suyuti) and says its theme is life after bodily death, resurrection, and final judgment.
rows.anchor: the continuation of human life after bodily death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conventional title comes from the word naba in verse 2.
rows.anchor: Its conventional title is derived from the word naba appearing in the second verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nature's evidence of purpose points to a conscious Creator who made nothing without purpose; the sequence anticipates judgment on whether people follow moral standards known through instinct and revelation.
rows.anchor: the overwhelming evidence of purpose and plan in all observable nature points to the existence of a conscious Creator

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad connects this passage with vv.4-5 and note 6 on 78:13.
rows.anchor: This passage connects with verses 4-5.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This late Meccan surah was revealed shortly after surah 78 and is named for an-nazi'at in its first verse.
rows.anchor: THIS late Meccan surah, revealed shortly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase min dhikraha literally asks what relation the Prophet has to stating the Hour.
rows.anchor: with regard to stating it (min dhikraha)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hour's 'utmost limit' is the beginning and end of all that can be known about it, as 7:187 also indicates.
rows.anchor: the beginning and the end of all that can be known about it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like several other verses, this indicates that earthly time is an illusory concept that loses meaning in the ultimate reality of the hereafter.
rows.anchor: a subtle indication of the illusory, earthbound nature of man's concept of "time" - a concept which, we are told, will lose all its meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This very early Meccan surah is named for its opening verb; the first ten verses were occasioned by an incident witnessed by the Prophet's contemporaries.
rows.anchor: The immediate cause of the revelation of the first ten verses was an incident witnessed by a number of the Prophet's contemporaries

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This very early surah, probably seventh in revelation order, takes its designation from kuwwirat in verse 1 and depicts the Last Hour and resurrection symbolically.
rows.anchor: this very early surah (most probably the seventh in the order of revelation) is derived from the verb kuwwirat

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since this surah follows surah 82 in revelation order, Asad considers it probably one of the last Meccan revelations.
rows.anchor: immediately after surah 82 (Al-Infitar)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad calls this the tenth surah in revelation order and says its designation comes from daybreak in verse 1.
rows.anchor: the tenth in the order of revelation - is based on the mention of "the daybreak" in the first verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night running its course alludes to spiritual darkness disappearing when a person becomes conscious of God.
rows.anchor: An allusion to the night of spiritual darkness which is bound to "run its course" - i.e., to disappear - as soon as man becomes truly conscious of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath is solemn evidence for God's existence and oneness.
rows.anchor: a convincing evidence of the existence and oneness of God

rows.speaker: Suyuti
rows.claim: Suyuti places the surah in the middle of the Meccan period, after surah 50.
rows.anchor: Although Suyuti places this surah in the middle of the Mecca period (after surah 50)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad considers it more likely that the surah belongs to the earliest years of Muhammad's prophethood.
rows.anchor: it is most probable that it belongs to the earliest years of Muhammad's prophethood

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kabad combines pain, distress, hardship, toil, and trial, requiring a compound translation.
rows.anchor: The term kabad, comprising the concepts of

rows.speaker: Ikrimah and Razi
rows.claim: Ikrimah, as cited by Baghawi, and Razi explain freeing a neck as freeing oneself from sin's burden.
rows.anchor: Thus lkrimah, as quoted by Baghawi; also Razi.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, fakk raqabah can mean freeing a human being from bondage, including social, economic, or political subjugation and exploitation describable as slavery.
rows.anchor: Alternatively, the phrase fakk raqabah may be rendered as "the freeing of a human being from bondage"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is identified by its first verse's key word and is generally assumed to have followed surah 97 soon after.
rows.anchor: It is generally assumed that it was revealed shortly after surah 97 (Al-Qadr).

rows.speaker: Al-Farra
rows.claim: Al-Farra says the moon follows the sun by deriving its light from it.
rows.anchor: Al-Farra, who lived in the second century after the hijrah, "the meaning is that the moon derives its light from the sun"

rows.speaker: Raghib
rows.claim: Raghib gives the same interpretation of the moon's following the sun.
rows.anchor: This is also Raghib's interpretation of the above phrase.

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari takes the pronoun 'it' to indicate the world or the earth.
rows.anchor: a pronoun apparently indicating "the world" or "the earth" (Zamakhshari)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first ten verses stress physical and spiritual polarity in creation, in contrast with the Creator's oneness and uniqueness.
rows.anchor: verses 1-10 stress the polarity - both physical and spiritual - inherent in all creation and contrasting with the oneness and uniqueness of the Creator.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is unanimously considered one of the earliest revelations, probably ninth in chronological order, and is named for the night mentioned in verse 1.
rows.anchor: UNANIMOUSLY regarded as one of the very early revelations - most probably the ninth in the chronological order

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People pursue good or bad ends, so their actions necessarily lead to divergent consequences, as also suggested at 91:8.
rows.anchor: at good and bad ends (cf. note 6 on 91:8) - sc., "and so the consequences of your doings are, of necessity, divergent"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ultimate good is an absolute moral value independent of time and social circumstance, a moral imperative.
rows.anchor: in moral values independent of time and social circumstance and, hence, in the absolute

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad points to note 6 on 87:8 for this phrase.
rows.anchor: See note 6 on 87:8.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links the claim of self-sufficiency with 96:6-7.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase may be rendered as a statement: his wealth will be of no avail when he falls.
rows.anchor: Or (as a statement): "of no avail will be to him his wealth when he..."

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Male and female differentiation and the night/day, darkness/light polarity in nature point to divergent human aims, echoing the first ten verses of the preceding surah.
rows.anchor: This, together with the symbolism of night and day, darkness and light, is an allusion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A story says revelation paused after surah 89 and Meccan opponents taunted the Prophet that God had forsaken and scorned him; Asad regards the report as doubtful.
rows.anchor: Whether or not we accept this somewhat doubtful story

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beyond the Prophet, the surah consoles any faithful person enduring hardship and sorrow that can lead even the righteous to question God's justice.
rows.anchor: every faithful man and woman suffering from the sorrows
